summary: John Burton-Page worked in Indology, archaeology, and linguistics. Educated at the Royal College of Music, Oxford, and Deccan College, he served as lecturer and Reader at SOAS (1950; 1971–1982) and held posts at Deccan College and the Royal Asiatic Society.
John C. Huntington was a scholar of history, archaeology, Buddhist studies, and Tibetology. He served as a professor at Ohio State University (attested 1987–1990 and 2000–2011).

John C. Maraldo worked in philosophy, Buddhist studies, and Japanology. He served at the University of North Florida, where he was attested in 1988 and later attested as distinguished professor emeritus of philosophy in 2015.

John Campbell Oman worked in Indology and religious studies. After serving in the Public Works Department (1866–1877), he was a professor at Government College University, Lahore (1877–1897), and principal of Khalsa College (1898–1899).
John Capper was an Indologist and historian. He founded The Ceylon Magazine in 1840 and served as editor of the Ceylon Times from 1858 to 1874.
John Carnac Morris worked in Indology and linguistics. He studied at the East India Company College from 1815 to 1817 and entered the Madras Civil Service in 1818.
John Caspar Leyden was an Indologist and linguist who studied at the University of Edinburgh (~1790–1797). In 1808, he was appointed professor of Hindustani at Fort William College.

John Chadwick worked in linguistics and classical archaeology. Educated at St Paul's School, Corpus Christi College, and Cambridge, he held Cambridge lectureships from 1952, served as Laurence Reader in Classics (1969–1984), and was a Fellow of Downing College.

John Clark Archer was a scholar of religious studies and Indology. Educated at Hiram College and Yale University, he spent his career at Yale (1914–1950), becoming Hocker Professor of Comparative Religion, and held a post at Khalsa College (1937).
John Clark Marshman worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He founded Serampore College in 1818 and directed the affairs of the Serampore Mission beginning in 1819.

John Claude White worked in Tibetology, history, and archaeology. He studied at Rugby School and the Royal Indian Engineering College before joining the Bengal Public Works Department as an assistant engineer in 1876.

John Clifford Holt is a scholar of Buddhist and religious studies. Educated at Gustavus Adolphus College, GTU, and the University of Chicago under Stanley Jeyaraja Tambiah, he served as Professor of Religion at Bowdoin College (1978–2019).
John Cockburn Thomson was an Indologist who completed his B.A. at Trinity College, Oxford (1852–1857). He studied under Christian Lassen (~1851–1853) and Horace Hayman Wilson (1852–1857).

John Collinson Nesfield was an Indologist and linguist educated at Highgate School and Merton College, Oxford. He taught at Highgate, Presidency University, and Krishnagar Government College, later serving as principal of Sampurnanand Sanskrit University (1878).
John Correia-Afonso was an archaeologist and historian who studied under Henry Heras from ~1948 to 1953 and later succeeded him.

John Corrigan is a scholar of religious studies who earned his Ph.D. at the University of Chicago. He taught at the University of Virginia and Arizona State University before becoming chair of the Department of Religion at Florida State University (~2001).

John Crawfurd was a linguist and historian who studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh (~1800–1803). He served as a physician for the East India Company (1803–1808) and succeeded Stamford Raffles in 1823.
John Cripps Pembrey was a scholar of linguistics and Indology who served as an Oriental Reader at the Clarendon Press, attested in 1904 and 1916.
Sir John Cumming was an Indologist and historian educated at the University of Glasgow and Balliol College, Oxford. He served as Vice-Chairman of SOAS University of London from 1925 to 1946.
John D'Oyly was a scholar of Indology and linguistics who completed his higher education at Corpus Christi College, University of Cambridge, graduating with a B.A. (~1792–1796).
